families.s: HSE Construction (Design and Management) dutyholder guidance
families.t: client, designer, contractor and principal-contractor duties for planning, competence, coordination and construction-phase control
f: A principal contractor is appointed by the client to control the construction phase of a project involving more than one contractor.
Principal contractors must plan, manage, monitor and coordinate the entire construction phase.
A written construction phase plan must be prepared before construction begins and kept under review.
Principal contractors must provide suitable welfare, site induction and measures against unauthorised access.
Commercial clients must make suitable project-management arrangements and appoint organisations with the required skills, knowledge, experience and capability.
Commercial clients must provide relevant pre-construction information to designers and contractors.
Contractors must plan, manage and monitor their work while controlling risks to workers and other people, including the public.
Design decisions can affect construction workers, building users and people who maintain, refurbish or demolish the asset.
families.g: CDM performance depends on project scope, number of contractors, appointments, competence, pre-construction information, design decisions, construction-phase planning, coordination and review.

families.t: toilets, washing, changing, eating, rest, maintenance and remote-site welfare provision
f: Construction workers must have access to toilets and facilities for washing, changing, eating and rest.
Commercial clients must ensure welfare arrangements exist, while contractors must provide facilities for workers under their control.
Principal contractors must ensure suitable welfare is available from the start of the project until it finishes.
Schedule 2 of CDM 2015 identifies minimum construction-site welfare facilities.
Facility type and number should reflect the size and type of work and may need to control hazardous-substance risks.
Facility location should account for cleaning access, travel time and remote parts of larger sites.
Toilets and washing facilities must be adequate, accessible and maintained with necessary supplies.
Changing, eating and rest arrangements should be suitable for the work, workforce and contamination risks.
families.g: Welfare adequacy depends on workforce size, work duration, location, travel time, hazardous substances, sex-specific needs, cleaning, water, drainage and maintenance arrangements.

families.s: HSE temporary-works design and management guidance
families.t: design, coordination, checking, loading, modification and removal of temporary works
f: Temporary works enable permanent works to be built and are usually removed after use.
Examples include access scaffolds, props, shoring, excavation support, falsework and formwork.
Some temporary works, such as haul-road foundations or crane platforms, may be incorporated into permanent works.
Temporary works require the same degree of care in design and construction as permanent works.
Temporary-works management must coordinate design, equipment selection, contractors, supervision, completion checks, loading authorisation and removal.
BS 5975 describes an accepted management approach using a Temporary Works Coordinator, although the job title is not itself a legal requirement.
Standard solutions are suitable only when site conditions and all design assumptions have been checked.
Construction sequence, systems of work and nearby activities must not damage or compromise temporary works.
families.g: Temporary-works safety depends on design assumptions, ground and loading, competence, coordination, checking category, installation, inspection, modification, loading authorisation and removal sequence.

families.s: HSE construction public-protection and site-security guidance
families.t: site boundaries, access control, falling objects, excavations, plant interfaces and vulnerable members of the public
f: Construction businesses must conduct work without putting members of the public and other affected workers at risk.
Client pre-construction information should cover boundaries, adjacent land use, access and exclusion of unauthorised people.
Every construction site requires managed boundaries and steps to exclude unauthorised access.
Falling tools or materials outside the site boundary can seriously injure members of the public.
Public risks also include falling into trenches and being struck by moving plant or vehicles.
Site fencing must reflect the work, surroundings, local population and likelihood that children will be attracted to the site.
The principal contractor must take reasonable steps to prevent unauthorised site access.
Children, older people and some disabled people may require additional planning and protection.
families.g: Public-protection needs depend on site boundaries, neighbouring land use, population, vulnerable groups, access points, excavations, falling-object potential, plant routes, work hours and security maintenance.

families.s: HSE underground-service and buried-cable avoidance guidance
families.t: planning, service information, locating, identification, safe digging and response to buried-service damage
f: A safe excavation system near underground services has three basic elements: planning, locating and identifying services, and safe excavation.
Damage to underground electrical cables can cause fatal or severe injury through arcing, explosion, flames and electric shock.
Safe work near buried cables should combine planning, cable plans, locating devices and safe digging practices.
The client and principal designer should provide available pre-construction information about underground services.
Underground electrical cables may resemble pipes and cannot be assumed dead by visual inspection.
Plans should guide the search but should be used with a suitable locating device to pinpoint services.
People using cable-locating equipment should understand detection techniques and the equipment's limitations.
Previously damaged but unreported cables can remain hazardous and later cause incidents.
families.g: Underground-service risk depends on service type and condition, record accuracy, locator capability, operator competence, excavation method, depth, ground conditions, isolation options and damage-response arrangements.

families.s: HSE overhead-electric-line avoidance and work-control guidance
families.t: line identification, owner consultation, avoidance, diversion, isolation, access control and work beneath live lines
f: Work near overhead electric lines must be planned and carried out to avoid danger from contact or close proximity.
Precautions are required even when work near a line is of short duration.
Excavators, MEWPs, scaffold poles, tipper vehicles, cranes and other high or long equipment create particular risk.
A dangerous flashover can occur without physical contact with a live conductor.
Overhead lines should be assumed live unless their owner proves otherwise.
Line owners should be consulted early enough to discuss diversion, isolation or other precautions.
The preferred hierarchy is avoidance, diversion or making the line dead.
Where danger cannot be eliminated, barriers, defined passageways, goal posts, warnings and controlled work are required.
families.g: Overhead-line risk depends on voltage, clearance, plant dimensions and movement, access routes, weather, line sag, ground levels, operator visibility, barriers and coordination with the network owner.

families.s: HSE excavator and quick-hitch safety guidance
families.t: attachment coupling, verification, control isolation, exclusion, lifting, inspection and operator competence
f: A quick hitch is a latching device that lets an excavator operator change buckets or other attachments rapidly.
Fatal incidents involving semi-automatic quick hitches led industry to move away from their supply.
A quick hitch is work equipment and must be suitable, maintained and used safely under work-equipment requirements.
The attachment-locking process must be completed and verified before the excavator is used.
Safety-control levers or isolation devices should prevent inadvertent operation of excavator controls when people are exposed nearby.
Excavator work requires control of the swing radius and exclusion of people from attachment and counterweight danger zones.
Using an excavator for lifting introduces additional risk and requires suitable examination and lifting controls.
Operators and people directing excavator work need appropriate competence, communication and supervision.
families.g: Excavator and quick-hitch risk depends on hitch type and condition, locking verification, attachment compatibility, control isolation, visibility, exclusion zones, lifting use, maintenance and operator competence.

families.s: HSE telescopic-handler selection, operation and maintenance guidance
families.t: operator authorisation, load stability, attachments, visibility, pedestrian control, inspection and lifting-person restrictions
f: Telehandler drivers should be trained, competent and authorised for the specific machine they operate.
Pedestrians need instruction on safe routes and how to make drivers aware of their presence.
Daily visual checks, regular inspections and servicing should follow manufacturer instructions and vehicle risks.
Safety-critical defects should be corrected promptly and the machine taken out of service when necessary.
Attachments must be compatible with the telehandler and suitable for the intended task.
Loads, boom extension, ground conditions, gradients and stabilisers affect telehandler stability.
People must not be lifted in a telehandler bucket or other unsuitable attachment.
Cab damage or missing protective glazing can expose operators to crushing or entrapment hazards.
families.g: Telehandler risk depends on machine configuration, load and reach, attachments, ground and slopes, visibility, pedestrians, stabilisers, maintenance, cab integrity and operator competence.

families.s: HSE ATV, quad-bike and side-by-side vehicle guidance
families.t: helmet use, active riding, maintenance, loads, route planning, training, passengers and rollover protection
f: Quad bikes and side-by-side vehicles can rapidly become unstable when used carelessly or in unsuitable conditions.
Many quad-bike fatalities involve head injury, and riders should always wear a suitable helmet.
The long seat on a sit-astride quad bike is for active riding and not for carrying passengers.
Checks should include tyre pressures, brakes, throttle and maintenance required by the manufacturer.
Rack loads must be secured, evenly balanced and kept within capacity.
Routes should be planned and unfamiliar routes walked to identify hidden obstructions and terrain hazards.
All riders require adequate training for the machine and tasks.
Children under 13 are prohibited from using an ATV at work and must not be carried as passengers.
families.g: ATV risk depends on vehicle type, terrain and gradient, weather, speed, load and attachments, tyre condition, helmet or restraint use, rider training and passenger practices.

families.t: handling facilities, race and crush design, restraint, animal temperament, maintenance and worker competence
f: Handling cattle always involves risk from crushing, kicking, butting or goring.
Suitable handling facilities should include a race and crush appropriate for the animals.
Workers handling livestock should be trained and competent.
Temperamental animals should be identified and managed through a rigorous culling policy.
Risk is greater with animals that are unfamiliar with handling, newly calved or involved in veterinary work.
Stock tasks on unrestrained cattle or with makeshift equipment are particularly hazardous.
A crush should restrain the head and body, be secured, provide safe working space and have a slip-resistant floor.
An unsecured animal must not wait directly behind an animal being worked on in the crush.
families.g: Livestock-handling risk depends on species and temperament, familiarity, calving and health, task, facility layout, restraint, lighting and flooring, escape routes, maintenance and handler competence.
